title: Esme's Perfect Butterfly
markdown:
The evening sky was soft with colours like lavender and rose. In the warm cozy garden, sleepy bumblebees were finding their soft nests. Esme the little scientist hummed a soft tune. Beside her, Tumble the tortoise, with his very patient eyes, blinked slowly. They had a special job to do before the garden party.

“We are making a butterfly banner for our party, Tumble,” Esme whispered, her voice as gentle as leaves in a soft breeze. “It needs to be the most lovely banner ever, to welcome all our friends.”

They had carefully cut out a big lovely shape from colourful paper, a shape meant to be a giant happy butterfly. But oh, the wings.

“Look, Tumble,” Esme sighed, holding up the paper. Her small shoulders slumped just a little. “This side is a little bit wiggly, and this side is a little bit round. They don’t look like they match, do they? They don’t feel like a pair.”

Tumble gave a slow thoughtful nod. The butterfly looked a little wobbly, not like the perfect butterflies they sometimes saw dancing on the warm air. They tried to trim one wing to match the other, snipping a little here and there, but it was not easy work. Neither side looked quite right.

Esme leaned back, her forehead wrinkled just a little. She looked around the peaceful garden, slowly over the leaves and the sweet-smelling flowers. Her eyes found a lovely pink flower. Its petals were opening gently in the fading light. She saw how the petals on one side of the middle part were just like the petals on the other side. They looked like they were looking at each other in a mirror.

“Oh!” Esme whispered. Her eyes lit up like a tiny firefly blinking. “Tumble, look! This flower is like a mirror, but it’s all one beautiful piece.” She gently touched the soft petals. “The left side is exactly, perfectly like the right side. They are a happy pair.”

A good idea started to grow in Esme’s mind, as soft and gentle as a moonbeam. “What if we only drew one side of the butterfly’s wing, right on the edge of the paper? And then we could fold the paper exactly in the middle. Then, when we cut along the line we drew, both sides would be exactly the same.”

Tumble gave a slow thoughtful blink. It sounded like a very clever idea.

With great care, Esme took a crayon and drew half of a beautiful butterfly wing, with graceful curves. Then she folded the paper butterfly exactly in the middle, making sure the drawn line lay right on the fold, like two sleepy halves snuggling together. With a tiny pair of child-safe scissors, that made a soft whispery sound, she began to snip, carefully following the line she had drawn. Snip, snip, snip.

When she unfolded the paper, she let out a happy little gasp. There, on both sides of the fold, were two perfectly matching wings. They looked so lovely, so balanced and beautiful, just like the petals of the pink flower. It was a perfect pair.

Dr. Pine, who had been quietly watering the sleepy lavender bushes nearby, smiled warmly. “Well done, Esme. You’ve discovered something quite wonderful today.”

Esme beamed, holding up the perfect butterfly. “One side is a mirror of the other. Symmetry.”

Dr. Pine nodded gently, his eyes twinkling. “That’s right, Esme. Symmetry means that one side is a mirror image of the other, a perfect reflection. You see it in the leaves that flutter in the breeze, and in the way you cut your butterfly’s wings so they match.”

Tumble gave a happy rumbling sound from deep within his sturdy shell. The butterfly banner, with its perfectly symmetrical wings, was going to be the most beautiful banner ever. A few early stars began to peek out. Esme pinned the banner where the guests would see both wings at once, left matching right, and Tumble settled beside her, slow and pleased, while the lavender still smelled of the watering.
